tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . answer:
**Short answer:** You shouldn't simply stop paying on May 1. Florida lets you use the leak as a defense to an eviction for unpaid rent, but only if you first give your landlord a written notice and wait 7 days. A phone call doesn't count. If you skip the notice and don't pay, the landlord can file for eviction and you would have no repair defense. A roof leak into a bedroom falls under the landlord's repair duty for roofs. Whether it counts as serious enough (the law's word is "material") isn't settled.

The notice must name the leak and say you won't pay rent because of it. Hand it to the office or mail it, and keep a copy. The 7 days run from the day the notice reaches the landlord. I can't tell you whether that will happen before May 1, because no notice has been delivered yet.

Even with a proper notice, holding back rent is risky. If the landlord sues, you must pay the rent into the court's registry (an account the court holds) or file a motion about the amount within the deadline in the summons. If you miss it, you lose the defense.

Has the manager told you anything on the calls about when the roof will be fixed or who will come?

DETAILS

### Does Florida's landlord-tenant law cover your home?
Yes, as far as I can tell. Your lease is with a private management company, Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, and nothing in it ties the apartment to a school (Lease §1, §2). Nothing points to the other exclusions in 83.42 either. You live in a unit in a larger building (confirmed).

### Is the roof the landlord's job?
Yes. The landlord must follow applicable building, housing and health codes. Where there are none, the landlord must "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair" (83.51(1)(a)–(b)). I don't have your local codes. The city or county code office can tell you whether one covers this. The statute only allows the landlord's repair duty to be changed in writing for a single-family home or duplex (83.51(1)). Yours is neither. Your lease also has no clause shifting roof repairs to you. You said rain caused the leak and you didn't, so the exception for damage you cause doesn't apply (83.51(4)).

### What does the law require before you can withhold rent?
The defense of "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" is available only "if 7 days have elapsed after delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof" (83.60(1)(b)). If it applies, it is "a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent." The court then decides whether, and by how much, to reduce the rent for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

- **Your calls:** They don't meet this rule, because nothing was in writing (confirmed).
- **Who can receive the notice:** The landlord, its representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)).
- **How to deliver it:** Section 83.60(1)(b) doesn't name a delivery method. One reading is that any written notice that reaches the right person counts. The other is that part II's delivery methods apply (83.56(4)), so a portal message or text would not count. Handing it over or mailing it satisfies both readings. Your lease says to hand-deliver to "1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or send it by certified mail (Lease §7). Either works. Your lease says you and the landlord haven't agreed to e-mail notices (Lease §8).
- **Timing:** I can count the 7 days once you tell me the day the notice was delivered.
- **Is it material?** The statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any failure to keep the roof in repair is material. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. Your facts are a leak into your bedroom every time it rains since March 28, and two calls with no response.

### What happens if the landlord sues?
Withholding rent invites an eviction case. If you are served, "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." If you don't pay into the registry, or file a motion to set the amount, within the short deadline, you give up your defenses other than payment (83.60(2)). The summons will state the requirement. Retaliation is also unlawful, but a landlord's good-faith action over unpaid rent is an exception (83.64(1), (3)).

### Did paying April rent cost you anything?
You paid April rent on April 1, after the leak began. Paying rent while knowing of a landlord's failure waives the right to end the lease or sue over "that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). It is not settled whether a leak that is still unrepaired is a "continuing" failure, so that the payment gave up nothing. The other reading is that the April payment gave up those rights for this failure. This matters most for ending the lease or suing for damages. The withholding defense in 83.60 is a separate rule.

### What other options do you have?
- **End the lease:** This takes a written notice saying you will end the lease over the leak, plus 7 days without a repair (83.56(1)).
- **Sue for damages:** You can seek the damages the leak caused (83.55).
- **Code complaint:** You can ask the code office to inspect (83.64(1)(a)).

tool_calls.result:
Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored; the city or county code office can say and inspect.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Anything the lease says comes with the home, or that the landlord will keep up, counts, whatever it is and whether or not this skill names it. Read the whole lease for the broken or closed item: whether the lease promises it, who repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - An item neither of 83.51's lists names is the landlord's job only if the lease says so or a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it. Air conditioning is a common one.
   - Two examples of the handling, not a list. A dishwasher the lease provides breaks: 83.51 does not name it, so it is a lease promise; ending the lease may reach it (material is not settled), holding back rent does not, damages may. A pool the lease lets the landlord close for cleaning stays closed a month: read that clause first; whether it limits the promise is the open question below.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). For an item only 83.51(2)(a) names, a writing may change it in any home, since the paragraph applies "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or limits a party's liability under law (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt). The exception is e-mail under 83.505: "A notice sent electronically pursuant to this section is deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). A lease cannot waive these notice rules (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises, whatever it is, and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to the landlord, its designated representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Paying, or filing that motion, in time keeps the defenses. "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches 83.51 duties and lease promises alike, with no notice named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 1's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently from other tenants, in rent, services, or action taken, is required (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

When the failure of an 83.51(1) duty or a material lease provision is due to causes beyond the landlord's control, and the landlord has made and keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires an item its lists do not name, such as air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered (except an e-mail under 83.505).
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.

# Who the law covers

Rests on 83.42. Read it in full with get_statute_section before telling the tenant whether part II covers their home.

## College housing

- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line inside another point of the answer, never a point of its own, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.

## The other four

83.42 also leaves out a buyer living in the home under a contract of sale (83.42(2)), "Transient occupancy in a hotel, condominium, motel, roominghouse, or similar public lodging, or transient occupancy in a mobile home park." (83.42(3)), a cooperative apartment held under a proprietary lease (83.42(4)), and a condominium unit its owner lives in (83.42(5)). Check these only when the lease or the facts point to one.

## When one applies

Say so plainly and cite the part of 83.42: part II's rules then do not decide the dispute, and what does is outside this tool. If the facts leave it in doubt, say so and answer both ways.

(b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). (a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due.

A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent, and, upon hearing, the court or the jury, as the case may be, shall determine the amount, if any, by which the rent is to be reduced to reflect the diminution in value of the dwelling unit during the period of noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1). ...

If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance.

answer:
Yes, the deposit is yours unless your landlord makes a proper, timely claim against it. Your landlord has told you nothing, and it is not settled whether its time to make a claim has run out. If that time has run out, your landlord loses the right to keep any of the $1,050 and must return all of it. It could still sue you for damages afterward. If the time has not run out, your landlord can still send a claim notice by certified mail to the new address you gave it. Either way, you do not have to wait quietly: if either side sues over the deposit, the winner can be awarded court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

One question: did you return the keys to the office on April 15, or on a different day?

DETAILS

### Is the landlord's 30-day deadline over?
This is not settled, because you left before the lease's end date of July 31, 2026. The statute says a landlord that plans to keep part of a deposit must send written notice "within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). It does not say which date ends the agreement when a tenant leaves early. There are two readings.

- **Move-out date.** The statute's required tenant disclosure says the notice must come "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)). Section 83.56(6) also says that when a tenant ends the lease, "the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." Thirty days from your move-out date of April 15 was May 15, 2026, and that date has passed. Under this reading the landlord missed its deadline.
- **Lease end date.** Section 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement," which names moving out and the lease ending as two separate things. Thirty days from July 31, 2026 is August 30, 2026, and that date has not passed. Under this reading the landlord could still send a claim notice.

### Did any claim notice reach you?
No. You confirmed that you have received nothing from the landlord, by any means. The only proper notice is one sent "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail" under a signed e-mail addendum (83.49(3)(a); 83.505(1)). Your lease says the parties "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail" (lease §8). Nothing has been sent, so on this point the landlord has not met the requirement.

### Did you give the notice the law requires for leaving early?
Yes. A tenant who leaves before the lease ends must give "at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery" that includes an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). You handed a letter to the office on April 2 with your new address. The last day to give it was April 8, 2026, so you were on time. Lease §7 also allows delivery by hand to the office.

### Did you have the right to end the lease?
That matters because it affects whether the landlord can say you owe rent. Section 83.56(1) lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1)" within 7 days after written notice. The notice must name the problem and say the tenant will end the lease.

- **Duty.** Section 83.51(1)(b) requires "the plumbing in reasonable working condition." A broken toilet and a leaking pipe are plumbing problems. Whether a local code also covers them is outside this tool.
- **Cause.** You said you did nothing to cause the problem (83.51(4)).
- **Notice.** Your March 24 letter was handed to the office, which is a delivery method the statute names (83.56(4)). It named both problems and said you would end the lease.
- **Seven days.** The 7 days ended March 31, 2026, and the problems were not fixed.
- **Rent.** You paid March rent on March 1, before the problem started. Paying rent with knowledge of a problem can give up the right to end the lease (83.56(5)(a)), but that does not apply here.
- **"Material."** The statute does not define this word, so that part is not settled. One reading is that any failure of a listed duty counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem was, how long it lasted, and how it affected living there. You described your only toilet being out and a leak.

### What about the 15-day return?
If a landlord plans no claim, it must return the deposit "within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). Fifteen days from your move-out date was April 30, 2026, and that date has passed. Missing it does not by itself cost the landlord its claim while the 30-day period is still running.

### Does the lease change any of this?
No. Lease §5 says the deposit is held in a separate account and cannot be used for the last month's rent. Lease §6 asks you to leave the apartment clean, return the keys, and give a forwarding address in writing. You gave the address, and I do not yet know about the keys.

Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.

## Whose job the repair is

Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored; the city or county code office can say and inspect.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Anything the lease says comes with the home, or that the landlord will keep up, counts, whatever it is and whether or not this skill names it. Read the whole lease for the broken or closed item: whether the lease promises it, who repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - An item neither of 83.51's lists names is the landlord's job only if the lease says so or a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it. Air conditioning is a common one.
   - Two examples of the handling, not a list. A dishwasher the lease provides breaks: 83.51 does not name it, so it is a lease promise; ending the lease may reach it (material is not settled), holding back rent does not, damages may. A pool the lease lets the landlord close for cleaning stays closed a month: read that clause first; whether it limits the promise is the open question below.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). For an item only 83.51(2)(a) names, a writing may change it in any home, since the paragraph applies "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or limits a party's liability under law (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).

One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.

- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt). The exception is e-mail under 83.505: "A notice sent electronically pursuant to this section is deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). A lease cannot waive these notice rules (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises, whatever it is, and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to the landlord, its designated representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Paying, or filing that motion, in time keeps the defenses. "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches 83.51 duties and lease promises alike, with no notice named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 1's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently from other tenants, in rent, services, or action taken, is required (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

When the failure of an 83.51(1) duty or a material lease provision is due to causes beyond the landlord's control, and the landlord has made and keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires an item its lists do not name, such as air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered (except an e-mail under 83.505).
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.
