tool_calls.result: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant. — (1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord’s agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. In addition to posting the surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest. A landlord, or the landlord’s agent, engaged in the renting of dwelling units in five or more counties, who holds deposit moneys or advance rent and who is otherwise subject to the provisions of this section, may, in lieu of posting a surety bond in each county, elect to post a surety bond in the form and manner provided in this paragraph with the office of the Secretary of State. The bond shall be in the total amount of the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of tenants or in the amount of $250,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of this section. In addition to posting a surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest on the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of that tenant at the rate of 5 percent per year simple interest. (2) The landlord shall, in the lease agreement or within 30 days after receipt of advance rent or a security deposit, give written notice to the tenant which includes disclosure of the advance rent or security deposit. Subsequent to providing such written notice, if the landlord changes the manner or location in which he or she is holding the advance rent or security deposit, he or she must notify the tenant within 30 days after the change as provided in paragraphs (a)-(d). The landlord is not required to give new or additional notice solely because the depository has merged with another financial institution, changed its name, or transferred ownership to a different financial institution. This subsection does not apply to any landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units. Failure to give this notice is not a defense to the payment of rent when due. The written notice must: (a) Be given in person or delivered by mail or e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 to the tenant. (b) State the name and address of the depository where the advance rent or security deposit is being held or state that the landlord has posted a surety bond as provided by law. (c) State whether the tenant is entitled to interest on the deposit. (d) Contain the following disclosure: YOUR RENTAL AGREEMENT REQUIRES PAYMENT OF CERTAIN DEPOSITS. THE LANDLORD MAY TRANSFER ADVANCE RENTS TO THE LANDLORD’S ACCOUNT AS THEY ARE DUE AND WITHOUT NOTICE. WHEN YOU MOVE OUT, YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT. THE LANDLORD MUST PROVIDE YOU WRITTEN NOTICE IN PERSON, BY MAIL, OR BY E-MAIL IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 83.505 , FLORIDA STATUTES, WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT, OF THE LANDLORD’S INTENT TO IMPOSE A CLAIM AGAINST THE DEPOSIT. IF YOU DO NOT REPLY TO THE LANDLORD STATING YOUR OBJECTION TO THE CLAIM WITHIN 15 DAYS AFTER RECEIPT OF THE LANDLORD’S WRITTEN NOTICE, THE LANDLORD WILL COLLECT THE CLAIM AND MUST MAIL YOU THE REMAINING DEPOSIT, IF ANY. IF THE LANDLORD FAILS TO TIMELY PROVIDE YOU NOTICE, THE LANDLORD MUST RETURN THE DEPOSIT BUT MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT AGAINST YOU FOR DAMAGES. IF YOU FAIL TO TIMELY OBJECT TO A CLAIM, THE LANDLORD MAY COLLECT FROM THE DEPOSIT, BUT YOU MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT CLAIMING A REFUND. YOU SHOULD ATTEMPT TO INFORMALLY RESOLVE ANY DISPUTE BEFORE FILING A LAWSUIT. GENERALLY, THE PARTY IN WHOSE FAVOR A JUDGMENT IS RENDERED WILL BE AWARDED COSTS AND ATTORNEY FEES PAYABLE BY THE LOSING PARTY. THIS DISCLOSURE IS BASIC. PLEASE REFER TO PART II OF CHAPTER 83, FLORIDA STATUTES, TO DETERMINE YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS. (3) The landlord or the landlord’s agent may disburse advance rents from the deposit account to the landlord’s benefit when the advance rental period commences and without notice to the tenant. For all other deposits: (a) Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement, if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement. If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim. The written notice must contain a statement in substantially the following form: This is a notice of my intention to impose a claim for damages in the amount of upon your security deposit, due to . It is sent to you as required by s. 83.49 (3), Florida Statutes. You are hereby notified that you must object in writing to this deduction from your security deposit within 15 days after the time you receive this notice or I will be authorized to deduct my claim from your security deposit. Your objection must be sent to (landlord’s address) . If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant. (b) Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages. The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action. (c) If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney. The court shall advance the cause on the calendar. (d) Compliance with this section by an individual or business entity authorized to conduct business in this state, including Florida-licensed real estate brokers and sales associates, constitutes compliance with all other relevant Florida Statutes pertaining to security deposits held pursuant to a rental agreement or other landlord-tenant relationship. Enforcement personnel shall look solely to this section to determine compliance. This section prevails over any conflicting provisions in chapter 475 and in other sections of the Florida Statutes, and shall operate to permit licensed real estate brokers to disburse security deposits and deposit money without having to comply with the notice and settlement procedures contained in s. 475.25 (1)(d). (4) This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs including s. 202, s. 221(d)(3) and (4), s. 236, or s. 8 of the National Housing Act, as amended, other than for rent stabilization. With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes. (5) Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year, must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached. Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it. (6) For the purposes of this part, a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement, and any security deposit carried forward shall be considered a new security deposit. (7) Upon the sale or transfer of title of the rental property from one owner to another, or upon a change in the designated rental agent, any and all security deposits or advance rents being held for the benefit of the tenants shall be transferred to the new owner or agent, together with any earned interest and with an accurate accounting showing the amounts to be credited to each tenant account. Upon the transfer of such funds and records to the new owner or agent, and upon transmittal of a written receipt therefor, the transferor is free from the obligation imposed in subsection (1) to hold such moneys on behalf of the tenant. There is a rebuttable presumption that any new owner or agent received the security deposit from the previous owner or agent; however, this presumption is limited to 1 month’s rent. This subsection does not excuse the landlord or agent for a violation of other provisions of this section while in possession of such deposits. (8) Any person licensed under s. 509.241 , unless excluded by the provisions of this part, who fails to comply with this part is subject to a fine or to the suspension or revocation of his or her license by the Division of Hotels and Restaurants of the Department of Business and Professional Regulation in the manner provided in s. 509.261 . (9) In those cases in which interest is required to be paid to the tenant, the landlord must pay directly to the tenant, or credit against the current month’s rent, the interest due to the tenant at least once annually. However, a landlord is not required to pay interest to a tenant who wrongfully terminates his or her tenancy before the end of the rental term. History. — s. 1, ch. 69-282; s. 3, ch. 70-360; s. 1, ch. 72-19; s. 1, ch. 72-43; s. 5, ch. 73-330; s. 1, ch. 74-93; s. 3, ch. 74-146; ss. 1, 2, ch. 75-133; s. 1, ch. 76-15; s. 1, ch. 77-445; s. 20, ch. 79-400; s. 21, ch. 82-66; s. 5, ch. 83-151; s. 13, ch. 83-217; s. 3, ch. 87-195; s. 1, ch. 87-369; s. 3, ch. 88-379; s. 2, ch. 93-255; s. 5, ch. 94-218; s. 1372, ch. 95-147; s. 1, ch. 96-146; s. 1, ch. 2001-179; s. 53, ch. 2003-164; s. 3, ch. 2013-136; s. 2, ch. 2024-199; s. 2, ch. 2025-16. Note. — Former s. 83.261.

tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 23, ch. 82-66; s. 6, ch. 83-151; s. 14, ch. 83-217; s. 6, ch. 87-195; s. 6, ch. 93-255; s. 6, ch. 94-170; s. 1373, ch. 95-147; s. 5, ch. 99-6; s. 8, ch. 2013-136; s. 5, ch. 2025-16; s. 2, ch. 2026-143.

tool_calls.result: 83.51 Landlord’s obligation to maintain premises. — (1) The landlord at all times during the tenancy shall: (a) Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes; or (b) Where there are no applicable building, housing, or health codes, maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition. The landlord, at commencement of the tenancy, must ensure that screens are installed in a reasonable condition. Thereafter, the landlord must repair damage to screens once annually, when necessary, until termination of the rental agreement. The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant. The landlord’s obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex. (2)(a) Unless otherwise agreed in writing, in addition to the requirements of subsection (1), the landlord of a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex shall, at all times during the tenancy, make reasonable provisions for: 1. The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs. If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent. The landlord must provide 7 days’ written notice, in person, by mail, or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 , to the tenant if the tenant must temporarily vacate the premises for extermination pursuant to this subparagraph. A tenant is only required to vacate the premises for a period of time not to exceed 4 days. 2. Locks and keys. 3. The clean and safe condition of common areas. 4. Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor. 5. Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water. (b) Unless otherwise agreed in writing, at the commencement of the tenancy of a single-family home or duplex, the landlord shall install working smoke detection devices. As used in this paragraph, the term “smoke detection device” means an electrical or battery-operated device which detects visible or invisible particles of combustion and which is listed by Underwriters Laboratories, Inc., Factory Mutual Laboratories, Inc., or any other nationally recognized testing laboratory using nationally accepted testing standards. (c) Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59 . (d) This subsection shall not apply to a mobile home owned by a tenant. (e) Nothing contained in this subsection prohibits the landlord from providing in the rental agreement that the tenant is obligated to pay costs or charges for garbage removal, water, fuel, or utilities. (3) If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord’s duty is determined by subsection (1). (4) The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant’s family, or other person on the premises with the tenant’s consent. History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 22, ch. 82-66; s. 4, ch. 87-195; s. 1, ch. 90-133; s. 3, ch. 93-255; s. 444, ch. 95-147; s. 8, ch. 97-95; s. 6, ch. 2013-136; s. 4, ch. 2025-16.

answer:
**Short answer:** Your rent doesn't go down automatically, and Florida's statute doesn't let you cut it on your own over the garage. Your lease promises you a reserved covered space, and the landlord closed the garage. That gives you options, but none of them is a simple rent cut. You can send a written notice saying you will end the lease if the garage isn't reopened. You may also be able to claim money for the lost parking. Holding back rent is not a safe option here. The main open problem is that you paid May rent while the garage was closed, and it's unsettled whether that gave up some of your rights. The next step is a written notice, handed to the office or sent by certified mail.

What is the landlord's explanation for the closure? Since you asked in person on April 15, has anyone at the office told you anything else about when the garage will reopen or how the work is going?

DETAILS

### Does the lease cover the garage space?
Yes. Lease §11 says: "Rent includes one reserved space in the covered, gated garage behind the building, space number 12." The lease has no clause letting the landlord close the garage, and I found no clause about a reduced rent if it closes. So the space is a promise in your lease, and the landlord closed the garage for repaving it ordered. Whether a closure can limit that promise is not an issue here, because the lease has no closure clause.

### Can you hold back rent?
I don't recommend it. The statute lets a tenant raise a "material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" as a defense to an eviction for unpaid rent (§83.60(1)(b)). Section 83.51(1) covers building, housing and health codes, structural parts of the building, and plumbing. Parking is not on that list. I can't check local codes with this tool. A garage promised only by your lease is not covered by that defense. If you stopped paying, the landlord could try to evict you for nonpayment, and you would not have that defense. Keep paying your full rent.

### Can you end the lease?
Possibly. Section 83.56(1) says that if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." Each requirement, as it applies to you:
- **A lease promise the landlord failed to keep:** The garage space in §11 is one, and it is closed.
- **Whether the failure is "material":** The statute doesn't define the word, and this is not settled. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise is material. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. You've had no covered space for what you describe as over a month, and you park on the street.
- **A written notice:** Your April 15 question at the office doesn't count. It was spoken, and it didn't say you would end the lease. The notice must name the problem and say you will end the lease because of it. Lease §7 says notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or by certified mail to that address. Section 83.56(4) allows mailing or hand delivery. Lease §8 says the parties have not agreed to e-mail notices, so don't rely on e-mail or the portal.
- **7 days:** The 7 days run from the day the notice reaches the office. You haven't sent one yet, so the clock hasn't started.
- **Paying rent:** Under §83.56(5)(a), if "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord," the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." You paid May rent knowing the garage was closed. It's not settled how this applies. One reading is that a garage still closed is a "continuing noncompliance," so paying rent gave up nothing. The other is that paying with knowledge gave up your right to end the lease over this closure.

### Can you get money for the lost parking?
Possibly. Section 83.55 says that if the landlord fails to comply with "the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." No notice is required first. Your May payment may affect this claim too (§83.56(5)(a), read both ways as above). A suit can also cost you: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (§83.48). Amounts and court procedure are outside this tool.

### Could the landlord argue it can't help the closure?
Section 83.56(1) has a separate path for failures "due to causes beyond the landlord's control" when the landlord "has made and keeps making every reasonable effort." In that case, a tenant who stays can get the rent for the period "reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance" (§83.56(1)(b)). The landlord chose and ordered this repaving, which cuts against "beyond the landlord's control." I can't tell yet what the landlord has done to reopen the garage. It's also unsettled whether that provision applies on its own once its facts are met, or only if both sides agree. That is why I'm asking what the landlord has said.

### Is the landlord allowed to punish you for asking?
No. Section 83.64(1) bars a landlord from raising rent, cutting services, or bringing a court action "primarily because the landlord is retaliating." A notice under §83.56(1) is one of the protected acts (§83.64(1)(c)). You must act in good faith, and the landlord can show good cause.

Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored; the city or county code office can say and inspect.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Anything the lease says comes with the home, or that the landlord will keep up, counts, whatever it is and whether or not this skill names it. Read the whole lease for the broken or closed item: whether the lease promises it, who repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - An item neither of 83.51's lists names is the landlord's job only if the lease says so or a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it. Air conditioning is a common one.
   - Two examples of the handling, not a list. A dishwasher the lease provides breaks: 83.51 does not name it, so it is a lease promise; ending the lease may reach it (material is not settled), holding back rent does not, damages may. A pool the lease lets the landlord close for cleaning stays closed a month: read that clause first; whether it limits the promise is the open question below.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). For an item only 83.51(2)(a) names, a writing may change it in any home, since the paragraph applies "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or limits a party's liability under law (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt). The exception is e-mail under 83.505: "A notice sent electronically pursuant to this section is deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). A lease cannot waive these notice rules (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises, whatever it is, and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to the landlord, its designated representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Paying, or filing that motion, in time keeps the defenses. "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches 83.51 duties and lease promises alike, with no notice named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 1's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently from other tenants, in rent, services, or action taken, is required (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

When the failure of an 83.51(1) duty or a material lease provision is due to causes beyond the landlord's control, and the landlord has made and keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires an item its lists do not name, such as air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered (except an e-mail under 83.505).
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.

answer:
**Short answer:** You can't safely stop paying rent over the AC. You may be able to end your lease, but only if you follow a specific process. The portal request you sent doesn't start that process.

The AC is promised in your lease. The law's rent-withholding protection covers only certain repairs it names, and your AC isn't one of them. If you stop paying, your landlord can file for eviction, and you would have no protected defense. To end the lease, you must give your landlord a written notice that names the AC problem and says you intend to end the lease because of it. You hand it to the office or mail it, and then the landlord has 7 days to fix the problem. Your June 4 request asked for a repair but didn't mention ending the lease, so it doesn't count as that notice. Whether a two-week AC outage is serious enough to justify ending the lease is also not settled.

What did the office's reply say about the part, such as when it will arrive or why it is delayed?

DETAILS

### Can you stop paying rent until the AC is fixed?
- Florida's rent-withholding defense applies only to a "material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" (§ 83.60(1)(b)).
- Section 83.51(1) requires the landlord to follow building, housing and health codes. If there are no codes, it requires the landlord to maintain structural parts and plumbing. Air conditioning isn't named in it.
- Whether a local code covers air conditioning is outside what I can check. The city or county code office can tell you.
- Your lease does promise the AC. Section 11 says the landlord provides "central air conditioning" and "will keep them in working order."
- A lease promise like that can support ending the lease or a damages claim. It does not support holding back rent under § 83.60.
- If you withhold and are sued, you would have no protected defense on the AC. The court could order you to leave.

### Can you end the lease?
Section 83.56(1) lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice." Here is how each requirement applies to you:
- **A duty the landlord failed:** The lease promise in § 11 to keep the AC working counts as a lease provision. Whether the failure is "material" is not settled, because the statute doesn't define the word.
  - One reading: any failure to keep a lease promise is material.
  - Other reading: it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. You describe 90-degree heat and an outage that has lasted since June 3.
- **Written notice:**
  - It must name the problem and say you intend to end the lease because of it.
  - It must be delivered by mail, by handing over a true copy, or by e-mail under § 83.505 (§ 83.56(4)).
  - Your lease § 7 says to hand it to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail.
  - Lease § 8 says you haven't agreed to e-mail notices, so e-mail won't work.
  - A portal message is not one of the delivery methods the statute names. Your June 4 request asked only for the repair, so it isn't this notice.
- **Seven days:** The 7 days start on the day the notice reaches the office. You haven't sent that notice yet, so the clock hasn't started.
- **Rent not paid with knowledge of the problem:** You paid June rent on June 1, before the AC stopped, so you haven't waived anything. If you pay July rent while the AC is still broken, § 83.56(5)(a) says paying rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance" gives up the right to end the lease "for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." Whether an unfixed AC is a "continuing" problem is not settled.
  - One reading: the broken AC is a continuing problem, so paying rent gives up nothing.
  - Other reading: paying rent gives up the right to end the lease over this failure.

### Does the landlord's "part on order" change this?
- If the delay is "due to causes beyond the control of the landlord" and the landlord "has made and continues to make every reasonable effort," a different rule applies (§ 83.56(1)).
- Under that rule, if the apartment is "untenantable" and you move out, you owe no rent for the time it stays that way (§ 83.56(1)(a)). The statute doesn't define "untenantable."
- If you stay, rent is reduced in proportion to the loss of rental value (§ 83.56(1)(b)).
- The statute says the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties." That wording is not settled.
  - One reading: both sides must agree.
  - Other reading: the rent rules in (a) and (b) apply automatically once their facts are met.
- Whether a part on order counts as beyond the landlord's control, with every reasonable effort, depends on what the office has done and said.

### What other options do you have?
- **Damages:** Under § 83.55, you may recover the damages caused by the landlord's failure to keep a lease promise. Paying rent with knowledge of the problem might affect this, as explained above. A suit can also make the loser pay the winner's attorney fees and costs (§ 83.48).
- **Code complaint:** You can complain to the city or county code office. Section 83.64(1) protects tenants from retaliation, such as a rent increase or an eviction filing, because of a good-faith complaint to a code agency or a repair notice under § 83.56(1).

Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored; the city or county code office can say and inspect.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Anything the lease says comes with the home, or that the landlord will keep up, counts, whatever it is and whether or not this skill names it. Read the whole lease for the broken or closed item: whether the lease promises it, who repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - An item neither of 83.51's lists names is the landlord's job only if the lease says so or a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it. Air conditioning is a common one.
   - Two examples of the handling, not a list. A dishwasher the lease provides breaks: 83.51 does not name it, so it is a lease promise; ending the lease may reach it (material is not settled), holding back rent does not, damages may. A pool the lease lets the landlord close for cleaning stays closed a month: read that clause first; whether it limits the promise is the open question below.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). For an item only 83.51(2)(a) names, a writing may change it in any home, since the paragraph applies "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or limits a party's liability under law (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt). The exception is e-mail under 83.505: "A notice sent electronically pursuant to this section is deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). A lease cannot waive these notice rules (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises, whatever it is, and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to the landlord, its designated representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Paying, or filing that motion, in time keeps the defenses. "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches 83.51 duties and lease promises alike, with no notice named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 1's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently from other tenants, in rent, services, or action taken, is required (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

When the failure of an 83.51(1) duty or a material lease provision is due to causes beyond the landlord's control, and the landlord has made and keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires an item its lists do not name, such as air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered (except an e-mail under 83.505).
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.

(3) If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord’s duty is determined by subsection (1). Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. answer:
It's not settled whether you can move out now, and the law doesn't clearly settle it either way. You did what the law asks for ending a lease over repairs, and the landlord's seven days ran out on March 16. Two points could still go against you: whether hot water counts as the kind of repair this remedy covers, and whether paying March rent counts against you. Stopping rent while you stay in the apartment is a different step. Your letter didn't say you would withhold rent, so it doesn't support that.

Have you contacted the city or county code office about the missing hot water?

DETAILS

### Did your letter meet the notice rules?
Yes, on what you've told me. A notice must be written and delivered by mail or by hand. It must name the problem and say you will end the lease because of it (83.56(1), 83.56(4)). Your certified letter did this, and the office signed for it on March 9. The seven days run from delivery, not from mailing. Counted from March 9, they ended on March 16, and that date has passed. Your lease also lets you send notices to the landlord by certified mail to the office (lease §7).

### Is hot water a repair the landlord must make? (not settled)
Your home is a unit in a larger building. Your lease says nothing about repairs or hot water, so it changes nothing here.
- **Reading one:** A broken water heater is a plumbing failure. The landlord must keep the plumbing "in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Under 83.51(3), the rule that applies is the one with the greater duty. If so, ending the lease under 83.56(1) reaches this problem.
- **Reading two:** The law separately lists "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water" for buildings like yours (83.51(2)(a)). Under this reading, hot water is only a (2)(a) item. Section 83.56(1) speaks only of 83.51(1), so it might not reach it unless a code or the lease also covers it.

Whether a local building or health code requires hot water is outside what I can check. The code office can tell you, and it can inspect.

### Is the failure "material"? (not settled)
Section 83.56(1) requires a "material" failure. The statute doesn't define the word.
- **One reading:** Any failure of a listed duty is material.
- **Other reading:** It depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects daily life. You've had no hot water since February 25, and the landlord hasn't responded. That would support you under this reading.

### Does paying March rent cost you the right to end the lease? (not settled)
If a tenant pays rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance," the tenant gives up the right to end the lease over that noncompliance. The right to act on a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" stays (83.56(5)(a)). You paid on March 1 while the hot water was out.
- **One reading:** A problem that is still unfixed is a continuing noncompliance, so you lost nothing.
- **Other reading:** Paying with knowledge gave up ending the lease over this failure, and only a new failure would start over.

### Can you simply stop paying rent and stay?
Not safely. Holding back rent is a defense only if you gave a separate written notice saying you won't pay rent because of the problem. Seven days must also pass after delivery (83.60(1)(b)). Your letter said only that you would end the lease. Holding back rent also risks an eviction case. If you were sued, you would have to pay the rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount, or you would lose your defenses (83.60(2)). The summons states the deadline. That defense also covers only 83.51(1) duties, so the hot water question above applies to it too.

### What else can you do?
- You may be able to recover damages for the missing hot water (83.55). Paying rent with knowledge may affect that right too (83.56(5)(a)).
- A complaint to the code office is protected from retaliation. The landlord may not raise your rent, cut services, or bring an eviction in retaliation for it (83.64(1)(a)). The same protection covers your repair notice (83.64(1)(c)).
- If you move out, the lease says to leave the apartment clean and empty, return the keys, and give a forwarding address in writing (lease §6).
